title: CATARACT 2, MULTIPLE TYPES
alt_titles: CATARACT 2, MULTIPLE TYPES, WITH OR WITHOUT MICROCORNEA

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that cataract-2 (CTRCT2), which comprises multiple types of cataract with or without microcornea, is caused by heterozygous mutation in the gamma-C-crystallin gene (CRYGC; 123680) on chromosome 2q33.3.

checks.claim: Cataract-2 (CTRCT2) comprises multiple types of cataract with or without microcornea.
checks.evidence_quote: there are four other mutations in CRYGC that have been associated with cataracts including Coppock-like cataracts (T5P), variable zonular pulverulent cataracts (5 bp duplication), lamellar cataracts (R168W), nuclear cataracts (R168W), and nuclear cataracts (C109X).
checks.explanation: The paper describes several CRYGC-related cataract types, and microcornea in this family. It does not use the CTRCT2 designation or describe the phenotype as 'with or without microcornea'.

checks.claim: Cataract-2 (CTRCT2) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the gamma-C-crystallin gene (CRYGC).
checks.evidence_quote: a 5-bp duplication within exon 2 of the gammaC-crystallin gene has been found in one allele of each affected family member and is absent from both unaffected family members and unaffected controls
checks.explanation: Paper supports a heterozygous CRYGC mutation causing cataract in one family; the general phenotype-wide causation claim goes beyond it.

checks.claim: The CRYGC gene is located on chromosome 2q33.3.
checks.evidence_quote: showed the heterozygous missense mutation c.502C>T in the CRYGC gene
checks.explanation: The chromosomal location is standard nomenclature added to the gene the paper names; the abstract itself does not give the location.

paragraphs.text: Cataract-2 is an autosomal dominant congenital cataract caused by mutation in the CRYGC gene. The lens opacities vary in type and include Coppock-like, zonular pulverulent, lamellar, and nuclear cataracts. In some families the nuclear cataract occurs with microcornea (Zhang et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2012).

checks.explanation: The paper reports autosomal dominant congenital cataract caused by CRYGC mutation.

checks.claim: The lens opacities in cataract-2 vary in type and include Coppock-like, zonular pulverulent, lamellar, and nuclear cataracts.
checks.evidence_quote: there are four other mutations in CRYGC that have been associated with cataracts including Coppock-like cataracts (T5P), variable zonular pulverulent cataracts (5 bp duplication), lamellar cataracts (R168W), nuclear cataracts (R168W), and nuclear cataracts (C109X).
checks.explanation: The paper lists all four cataract types.

checks.claim: In some families with cataract-2, nuclear cataract occurs with microcornea.
checks.evidence_quote: We report the identification of a four-generation Chinese family with a clear diagnosis of congenital nuclear cataracts and microcornea.

paragraphs.text: Scott et al. (1994) described a 7-generation family in which 48 of 138 individuals were known to have autosomal dominant congenital cataracts of the pulverulent type. Of 53 family members examined, 28 had congenital cataracts: 19 were unilateral (8 right eyes and 11 left eyes) and 9 were bilateral. On detailed slit-lamp examination, the clinically unaffected eye in unilateral cases had no lens opacity. When historical data were included, there were 48 affected members: 28 unilateral, 17 bilateral, and 3 obligate carriers who were not examined. Cataract severity varied within the family. At one extreme was a subtle unilateral zonular cataract with 20/20 vision. Other members had bilateral inner fetal nuclear pulverulent opacities with 20/16 vision in both eyes, and some had dense unilateral or bilateral nuclear cataracts that required early surgery. The authors reported that the autosomal dominant gene was expressed in an apparently random way as either unilateral or bilateral cataract. To their knowledge, this was the first such family described in the literature.

paragraphs.text: Zhang et al. (2009) studied a 4-generation Chinese family from a relatively isolated region of northern China in which 6 members had autosomal dominant congenital nuclear cataracts and microcornea. They had no other ocular or systemic abnormalities. The affected individuals had bilateral congenital nuclear cataracts, with a central nuclear opacity involving the embryonic, fetal, and infantile nucleus of the lens. They also had small eyeballs, and their corneas were about 9 to 10 mm in diameter. Every affected individual had visual acuity of hand movements in front of the eye, together with nystagmus and amblyopia.

paragraphs.text: Guo et al. (2012) described a 4-generation Chinese family in which 6 members had isolated bilateral autosomal dominant congenital nuclear cataracts and microcornea. The nuclear opacities involved the embryonic, fetal, and infantile nuclei. Corneal diameter was about 9 mm in all affected members. All patients had nystagmus and amblyopia, and their intraocular pressure was normal. There was no family history of related systemic abnormalities. The proband was diagnosed at age 8 years, and the other affected members were diagnosed between 6 months and 13 years of age.

(2009), autosomal dominant inheritance was supported by affected individuals in each of 4 generations and by male-to-male transmission, and penetrance appeared to be virtually complete.

paragraphs.text: Lubsen et al. (1987) studied a family with hereditary Coppock-like cataract using TaqI RFLPs within the gamma-crystallin gene cluster. A haplotype (P) was present only in family members with cataract, and all affected members carried it. This haplotype was not among those found in the Dutch and English populations. The finding showed close linkage between the gamma-crystallin gene cluster and the cataract locus, with a maximum lod score of 7.58 at theta = 0.

paragraphs.text: Zhang et al. (2009) carried out a genomewide linkage scan in a Chinese family with congenital nuclear cataract and microcornea. paragraphs.text: Brakenhoff et al. (1994) cloned the gamma-D and psi-gamma-E genes from the Coppock-like cataract (CCL) chromosome. The gamma-D gene functioned the same as its allele cloned from a wild-type chromosome. In contrast, the psi-gamma-E pseudogene (CRYGEP) from the CCL chromosome had a cluster of sequence changes within and around its TATA box. Together, these changes increased psi-gamma-E promoter activity tenfold, raising its expression to 30% of that of the gamma-D gene.

paragraphs.text: Heon et al. (1999) found that the Coppock-like cataract mutation previously reported in the CRYGE pseudogene was a polymorphism, present in 23% of their control population. Further analysis of the original Coppock-like cataract family identified a missense mutation in a highly conserved segment of exon 2 of the CRYGC gene. This mutation was not found in a large control population. The authors considered this the first evidence that CRYGC is involved in human cataract.

paragraphs.text: In a family with variable zonular pulverulent cataract, Ren et al. (2000) identified a heterozygous 5-bp duplication in exon 2 of the CRYGC gene. The duplication was present on one allele in every affected family member and was absent from unaffected family members and unaffected controls. The CRYGD gene showed no abnormalities. Ren et al. (2000) also sequenced the CRYGEP promoter region and carried out allele-specific oligonucleotide analysis in members of the pedigree. They concluded that activation of the gamma-E pseudogene was unlikely to cause the cataracts. Because base changes in the TATA box were also found in unaffected controls, these changes were excluded as a sole cause of cataract.

paragraphs.text: In affected members of a family with autosomal dominant nuclear congenital cataract, Gonzalez-Huerta et al. (2007) sequenced the CRYGA-D gene cluster. They identified a heterozygous c.502C-T transition in the CRYGC gene, resulting in an arg168-to-trp (R168W) substitution. The mutation segregated with the disease and was not found in healthy family members or in 170 unrelated controls. The variant was listed as a SNP in the NCBI database, but the authors concluded that R168W is the actual disease-causing mutation.
